title: Blood Relations
shortDescription: Build the family tree one clue at a time — and watch gender-specific terms, the exam's favourite distractor.
genZNote: Stop drawing the whole family tree in your head. Put the known person in the middle of the page and let each clue add a branch.

sections.heading: Core Idea
sections.body: Blood relation problems are solved by physically building a family tree/diagram from the stated relationships ONE CLUE AT A TIME, rather than trying to hold the whole chain in your head. Pick one person as the centre, then add each relative as they're introduced.

table.caption: These distinctions are the single most common blood-relations distractor — the exam swaps 'mother's brother' for 'father's brother' expecting you to skip past it.

steps.name: Pick a centre
steps.explanation: Choose the person the question ultimately asks about, or the first person mentioned, and place them in the middle of your scratch diagram.
steps.purpose: Gives every subsequent clue a fixed point of reference.

steps.name: Add one relative per clue
steps.explanation: Process the clues strictly in the order given, adding one box/line to the diagram per clue, marking gender where stated.
steps.purpose: Prevents the chain from becoming ambiguous halfway through — build incrementally, don't jump ahead.

steps.name: Read off the answer
steps.explanation: Once every clue is placed, trace the path from the centre to the person asked about and name the relationship using standard terms.
steps.purpose: The diagram makes the final relationship visually obvious instead of requiring you to re-trace the logic verbally.

sections.heading: Common Traps
bullets: Swapping maternal and paternal relations because the gendered wording was skimmed too fast.
Trying to resolve the whole chain mentally instead of sketching it — this is where multi-clue questions go wrong under time pressure.
Assuming a relationship is symmetric (e.g. 'A is B's brother' does not automatically make B 'A's brother' if B could be female — B would be A's sister).

sections.heading: Exam Strategy
bullets: Always sketch, even for a 3-clue question — the few seconds spent drawing save far more time than a mental mistake would cost.
Underline or circle every gendered word ('brother', 'sister', 'son', 'daughter') as you read the question, before starting the diagram.

quickRevision.oneLineDefinition: Blood relation questions are solved by building a family-tree diagram one clue at a time, not by mental tracking.
keyFacts: Mother's brother = maternal uncle. Father's brother = paternal uncle — the two are commonly swapped as a distractor.
Relationships are not automatically symmetric across gender — check who is male/female at each step.
commonConfusion: A relationship stated from one person's perspective does not automatically mirror the same word from the other person's perspective.

highYieldFacts: Gender-specific relation terms (maternal vs paternal) are the most-tested distractor in this topic.
commonTraps: Skimming past gendered wording and swapping maternal/paternal relations.
mustRemember: Build the family tree incrementally, one clue at a time — never try to hold the full chain in your head.
